name: Ainu and their ancestors
summary: The Indigenous people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, whose culture grew from the Epi-Jōmon and Satsumon cultures. Japan absorbed Hokkaido in 1869.

knownFor.label: Attus robes
knownFor.note: Cloth woven from elm bark, with bold patterns.

knownFor.label: Iyomante
knownFor.note: A ceremony sending a bear spirit back to the gods.

location.value: Hokkaido, the Tōhoku region of Honshu, Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands and other lands around the Sea of Okhotsk.

resources.value: Salmon, sika deer, brown bears, shellfish, seaweed and seals.

urbanisation.value: Small villages (kotan), usually of fewer than ten households, along rivers and coasts.

disease.value: Epidemic diseases such as smallpox reduced the population during the period of Matsumae trade.

migration.value: Their ancestors (Emishi) were pushed to the northern islands from the 9th century; later many were forced to move their villages near Japanese fishing grounds.

economicBase.value: Hunting, fishing and gathering, with some millet growing.

tradeRoutes.value: Transit trade between Honshu and Northeast Asia; the Matsumae clan held exclusive trading rights with the Ainu.

moneyAndTax.value: Trade with the Ainu was a Matsumae monopoly, later leased to Japanese merchants.

governmentType.value: Villages led by chiefs; no state.

keyRulers.value: Shakushain, who led a revolt in 1669.

succession.value: Chiefs often inherited their role through family lines.

institutions.value: The village head's house served as a public meeting place.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalries between regional chiefs are recorded in the 17th century, including the conflict that led to Shakushain’s revolt.

armyAndTech.value: Arrows and spears tipped with poison (surku) made from aconite.

territoryChange.value: Japan began developing Hokkaido in 1869; in 1875 Sakhalin went to Russia and the Kuril Islands to Japan.

inventions.value: Robes woven from bark fibre (attush) and poison-tipped arrows.

scienceEducation.value: Oral literature (Yukar), now designated Hokkaido Heritage.

openness.value: Traded with the Japanese and, on Sakhalin, paid tribute to Ming and Qing China; Ainu groups competed to import Japanese goods.

religion.value: Animist: everything in nature has a kamuy (spirit or god) inside.

languageWriting.value: Ainu is a language isolate; Hokkaido Ainu is likely extinct, though there are revival efforts.

artsArchitecture.value: Distinctive Ainu patterns, embroidered garments, bark-fibre robes and shaved wooden carvings (inau).

socialStructure.value: Small kotan villages of scattered families, with a village head.

sharedIdentity.value: Many still keep their Ainu identity and traditional ways ("Ainu puri").

dailyLife.value: Chise houses with wooden frames roofed with reeds, grass or bark; salmon was a staple food.

neighbours.value: Japanese, Russians, and the Nivkh and other peoples of Sakhalin and the Amur.

ideasReligions.value: Kept their animist beliefs; Meiji-era assimilation policies banned their religion and forbade their language in schools.

colonisation.value: Japan set up the Hokkaidō Development Commission in 1869; an 1899 act labelled the Ainu "former aborigines" to assimilate them.

riseSignals.value: The "Ainu culture period" followed the Satsumon culture, from around the 13th century.

peakPeriod.value: Before Japanese control tightened in the 18th century.

outcome.value: Recognised as Indigenous by Japan in 2019.
